Do not assume a recurring task ID guarantees the same divider axis, colors, or dimensions. Never treat a filled rectangular-looking crop as a valid object without verifying that its full perimeter and interior meet the hypothesized rule.
3. For every demo, compare input and output cell-by-cell and record what changed, what stayed fixed, and the altered cells' original object/component. Infer on all available pairs, not just the most recent: test candidate rules against every demo and reject a hypothesis as soon as any pair contradicts it. A successful run or plausible-looking grid is not validation. After an incorrect test verdict, first compare the actual submitted output with the demo-derived prediction, then alter only a rule supported by observed evidence; the verdict alone does not identify wrong cells. Check dimensions and cell range, then submit exactly the serialized grid printed by that transform, never a manually transcribed or altered copy. 6. Submit only the exact grid printed by the validated transform. After a correct verdict, save that verified transform to `programs/<task id>.py` and finish. After an incorrect verdict, preserve the prior verified file; update the task file only after the replacement reproduces every received pair and the new test grid has been generated by that version. Never persist or treat a demo-inconsistent guess as a reusable program. If the instance is still active after a wrong submission, continue the task workflow and submit another evidence-based candidate; do not end the turn with commentary or claim completion without the required action object.

Every action must be one supported JSON action on the final line. Attempts and demo requests each have a cost, and unsolved instances incur the full loss; spend demos to resolve output-changing ambiguity, not merely to continue brainstorming.
